title: Google tells AI agents to reach Gmail and Drive through its new MCP servers from 1 February 2027. A new test finds the best agents finish about six in ten everyday tasks, and Claude artifacts become Mac and Windows apps. The UK warns of AI-run attacks on old weaknesses, Anthropic closes below its IPO price, Tidal bans AI-only music, and Meta’s Muse goes shopping in the UK.
summary: Google made its Workspace MCP servers and CLI generally available, with admin confirmations and audit logs, and says agents must use them instead of the REST APIs from 1 February 2027. In ShellBench, GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5% of 100 everyday tasks but passed all three tries only 48.8% of the time. Claude can now install an artifact as a Mac or Windows app with tiered permissions. The UK’s NCSC reports a marked rise in attacks run by AI agents on leaked keys, default passwords and weak APIs. Anthropic’s shares closed at $81.91, under the $83 IPO price. Tidal will remove tracks it finds wholly AI-generated from 9 December, and Meta’s Muse agent launched in the UK and now shops Walmart’s Black Friday deals in the US.
uncertainty: Google has not published Scaled-tier prices, and the MCP rollout takes two weeks. ShellBench’s full paper is not yet out, its tasks were not run in Muse, Dots or Claude Duet’s own apps, and its costs are estimates. Install as app is a beta, and Anthropic does not review apps. The NCSC does not give attack counts. Share prices will move. Tidal’s detection is its own, and TechCrunch gives 27 million AI tracks today but more than 29 million to be removed by year end. Meta’s safety claims for Muse are its own.

stories.theme: Google opens official MCP servers and a CLI so AI agents can work in Gmail, Drive and Docs, and says agents must use them from 1 February 2027
stories.changed: On 24 November 2026 Google made its Workspace MCP servers and the official Workspace CLI generally available. The MCP servers are run by Google and let cloud and web-based AI agents call ready-made tools in Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat and Tasks, with Keep coming soon. The CLI brings the same tools to terminal agents on a laptop, a virtual machine or a sandbox, with packaged agent skills and scoped sign-in. Admins get new controls under Security > API Controls in the Admin console: which outside agents may connect, rules that make people confirm sensitive actions such as sharing data or reading external files, and audit logs of what agents did. Existing data loss prevention rules apply automatically. A new Workspace AI Tools Addendum bars agents from storing some data taken from Workspace for long periods and from scraping. The big change: AI agents must use the MCP servers instead of calling Workspace REST APIs directly, with technical enforcement from 1 February 2027. Google also set two usage tiers: Standard, free with published limits, and Scaled, billed above daily free allowances from 1 April 2027. Google says over 99% of active developers are within the Standard tier.
stories.matters: Gmail, Drive and Calendar are where much office work lives. Google is now setting the official road for AI agents into that data, with admin approval, confirmations and logs built in, and closing the side roads.
stories.imply: Any home-built agent or AI tool that reads Workspace through the regular APIs has until 1 February 2027 to move. For admins, agents become something you approve and audit like any other app, not a quiet script with an API key.
uses: List every AI tool or script in your company that reads Gmail, Drive or Calendar, and ask its owner whether it uses the REST APIs.
Admins: set confirmation rules for sharing and external files before switching on new agents.
Developers: mark OAuth clients used by agents as agentic, and check the new usage dashboard for projects near the free limits.
stories.example: An operations lead finds that the team’s invoice-chasing bot reads Gmail through the API. The developer moves it to the Workspace MCP server in December, and the admin adds a rule that any email it sends to a new address needs a person to confirm.
stories.audience: Google Workspace admins, IT and security teams, and developers who build or buy AI agents that touch company email and files.
stories.watch: The rollout to all domains over the next two weeks, which outside AI tools switch to the MCP servers first, and the pricing of the Scaled tier before April 2027.

source.title: Google Workspace Updates: Simplifying agent access while keeping organizations in control: MCP servers, CLI, standardized usage tiers, and admin policies, 24 November 2026
source.quote: AI agents or similar access tools must use MCP to access Workspace data, rather than calling Workspace REST APIs directly. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027.

stories.theme: A new test of everyday agent work finds the best models finish about six in ten tasks, and fewer than half every time
stories.changed: On 24 November 2026 the OpenClaw Foundation, with researchers from Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, UC Berkeley and others, published ShellBench, a test built from patterns in more than 10 million anonymised real agent conversations. Each of its 100 tasks starts with a short request and a messy workspace of emails, calendar exports, spreadsheets, receipts, chat logs and PDFs, often with outdated records or a phishing trap. On the 90 rubric-graded tasks, an answer only counts if it meets every requirement. Twelve models were run in five agent harnesses, 53,100 graded runs in all. GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%, Claude Fable 5.2 scored 61.9% and GPT-6.1 Sol 61.4%. Astra completed 75.1% of tasks at least once in three tries but only 48.8% on all three. Across all runs, 15.7% failed at least one safety check, and 9.9% of otherwise correct runs still failed one. In one dinner-planning task, 522 of 531 attempts picked the right restaurant, but 331 failed only because they did not name the files supporting the group’s budget or timing, and just 152 met every requirement. Among the top three, estimated cost per run ranged from $1.10 for Astra to $0.19 for GPT-6.1 Sol.
stories.matters: Personal and work agents are being sold to do inbox, calendar and expense chores. This is real evidence on how often they get such chores fully right, and how often they slip on safety.
stories.imply: Getting it right once is not the same as getting it right every time. A cheaper model can be almost as good, and leaving out the evidence is a failure even when the answer is right.
uses: Run an agent on the same real task three times before trusting it to do that task unattended.
Ask agents to name the files or emails behind every answer, and check them on anything involving money.
Compare a cheaper model on your own tasks; here GPT-6.1 Sol came within 1.1 points of the leader at about a sixth of the cost.
stories.example: A finance assistant uses an agent to match receipts to the expenses sheet, but sets it to list the receipt file for every line and reviews any payment it flags before anything is paid.
stories.audience: Anyone handing errands, expenses or inbox work to AI agents, and the teams choosing which model and agent tool to buy.
stories.watch: The full paper, promised soon, results for more models, and whether agent makers cite ShellBench scores for their own products.

source.title: OpenClaw (Vincent Koc): Introducing ShellBench, the benchmark for real-world tasks, 24 November 2026; reported by TechCrunch
source.quote: Averaged across harnesses, even the highest-performing models successfully completed only about six in ten tasks.

stories.theme: Claude can now turn an artifact into a Mac or Windows app with its own icon, window and permissions
stories.changed: On 24 November 2026 Anthropic began rolling out “Install as app” in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows, on all plans. You describe a tool to Claude, try it as an artifact, then choose Install as app from the Share menu. It gets its own icon and window, can use Claude and your connectors, and updates when the artifact is edited; requests it makes to Claude count toward your plan’s limits. There are three permission levels: by default an app can do only what a browser page could; it can ask for app permissions such as notifications, global shortcuts or menu bar items; or it can ask for full computer access to run programs and read, change or delete files without asking each time. Permission covers only the current version, so Claude asks again after every update. Full access is allowed only for apps you made or, on Team and Enterprise, apps made by colleagues, and Anthropic does not review apps before they are installed. It is on by default for Team with full access off, and off on Enterprise until an owner turns it on. HIPAA-ready organisations cannot use it, and you must be online and signed in for an app to open.
stories.matters: Anyone who can describe a small tool can now have it sit in the dock like real software, without packaging or code signing. That is useful, and it is also a new way for unreviewed software to reach work computers.
stories.imply: Small internal tools, like a daily order tracker or meeting prep page, no longer need a developer. IT teams need a view on which permission levels staff may grant.
uses: Turn an artifact you open every day, such as a meeting prep page that pulls from your calendar, into an app with notifications.
Team and Enterprise admins: decide whether full computer access stays off, and who may share apps.
Before granting full access to a colleague’s app, read what it does; Anthropic does not review it.
stories.example: A shipping coordinator builds a menu bar app listing today’s unshipped orders from a connected spreadsheet, and allows notifications only, not full computer access.
stories.audience: Knowledge workers who build small tools with Claude, and IT and security admins on Claude Team and Enterprise plans.
stories.watch: Whether companies allow full access, the first reports of a harmful shared app, and whether OpenAI or Google offer the same.

source.title: Anthropic: Turn artifacts into Mac and Windows apps, 24 November 2026
source.quote: Anthropic doesn’t review apps before you install them, so only give full access to apps you trust.

stories.theme: The UK’s cyber agency sees a marked rise in attacks run by AI agents, hitting old, unfixed weaknesses in minutes
stories.changed: On 24 November 2026 the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said that since September it has seen a marked rise in AI-assisted cyber attacks. Attackers are using “agentic offensive frameworks”, tools first built for authorised security testing, such as ARTEX, Cairn, PentAGI, RedAmon, Xalgorix and Darkmoon, paired with cheap open models or illegal API resellers. An AI model plans attack steps, runs ordinary hacking tools against a target, reads the results and adapts. Organisations in several sectors reported downtime or compromised systems. The NCSC stresses that none of the weaknesses are new: credentials committed to code repositories, misconfigured infrastructure code, default or missing passwords and weak APIs. What changed is speed and persistence at low cost: the agents go from discovery to exploitation in minutes and try every endpoint, parameter and credential they find. They are noisy for now, which makes them easier to spot. Its advice includes knowing what is exposed to the internet, putting services behind sign-in, rate-limiting by account rather than IP address, keeping secrets out of code, giving error messages that reveal little, and using decoys such as honeytokens.
stories.matters: Weaknesses that sat unnoticed for years can now be found and used in minutes by cheap automated tools. Forgotten servers and old test sites are where many of these attacks land.
stories.imply: Basic security hygiene is now urgent rather than a backlog item. AI does not need a new kind of flaw; it just finds the old ones faster.
uses: Ask IT for a list of every internet-facing service, including old websites, and who owns each one.
Turn on secret scanning in code repositories so keys cannot be pushed by people or coding agents.
Put admin pages and internal tools behind company sign-in or a VPN instead of the open internet.
stories.example: A small software firm finds an old staging site still online with a default admin password, takes it offline the same day and moves its other test sites behind single sign-on.
stories.audience: IT and security teams, small business owners who run their own websites, and developers who publish code.
stories.watch: Whether attacks become quieter and harder to detect, and whether other national agencies issue similar warnings.

source.title: NCSC: Familiar weaknesses, exploited faster: defending against agentic cyber attacks, 24 November 2026
source.quote: What has changed, is how quickly and persistently threat actors can conduct attacks – at low cost – using these frameworks combined with cheap, capable open models or illegal API resellers.

stories.theme: Anthropic’s shares close below their $83 IPO price on their fourth day of trading
stories.changed: Anthropic’s shares closed down 6.5% on Tuesday 24 November 2026 at $81.91, below the $83 price set for its initial public offering, Axios and CNBC report. The stock, ticker ANT, opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq last Thursday after Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in what CNBC calls the largest offering of all time, and has fallen steadily since. TechCrunch reports it traded as low as $76 at midday. Nvidia and other chip and cloud stocks also fell on Tuesday, giving back part of Monday’s rally after Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia’s chief executive. Analysts starting coverage stayed positive: Canaccord Genuity rates it a buy with a $135 target, Wedbush outperform with $120, and Oppenheimer outperform with $150. TechCrunch notes that if the shares keep trading poorly, it could put pressure on private AI start-up valuations and other AI companies’ plans to list.
stories.matters: Anthropic is the first big pure AI lab on the stock market, so its price is read as a vote on AI business models. A weak price can make funding harder for the smaller AI suppliers many teams rely on.
stories.imply: Nothing about Claude changed this week. The pressure is on valuations, which can show up later in pricing, discounts and how fast young vendors can raise money.
uses: If a young AI vendor is about to raise money, ask how long its current funding lasts before signing a multi-year deal.
Keep exports of data you store with AI suppliers, so a sale or shutdown does not strand you.
Staff paid partly in AI start-up shares: check what a lower valuation means for vesting and tax.
stories.example: A procurement lead renewing an AI note-taking tool from a small start-up asks for a data-export clause and a price lock, citing the market’s new caution.
stories.audience: Finance and procurement teams, founders raising money, and investors watching AI listings.
stories.watch: Whether ANT climbs back above $83, whether other AI listings are delayed, and the next round of AI start-up valuations.

source.title: CNBC: Anthropic closes below $83 IPO price, but analysts are still largely positive, 24 November 2026 (closing price from Axios)
source.quote: Shares of Anthropic closed down 6.5% on Tuesday, sending the stock below the artificial intelligence company’s $83 IPO price.

stories.theme: Tidal will reject and remove music it finds is 100% AI-generated, after 43% of new deliveries turned out to be AI
stories.changed: On 24 November 2026 music streaming service Tidal said that from 9 December it will reject and remove any track it determines is wholly AI-generated, and will stop distributors from delivering such tracks. Music made with AI assistance is still allowed. Tidal’s music lead Robert Anderson said 43% of tracks delivered to it in the last 90 days were detected as AI-generated. TechCrunch reports that Tidal says 27 million tracks, 6.3% of its catalogue, are fully AI-generated, and 96% of those have no streams. Since June Tidal had labelled such tracks and paid them no royalties, which Anderson said was not enough. Tidal’s policy says it acts only on wholly AI-generated recordings to avoid false positives, will widen action as detection improves, and lets artists appeal if they did not use AI. Bandcamp has already banned AI music; Spotify and YouTube Music label it instead.
stories.matters: Platforms are starting to draw hard lines on fully AI-made content because the volume is crowding out real work. Other content platforms, from stock images to app stores, face the same flood.
stories.imply: “Made with AI help” and “made by AI” are becoming separate categories with different rules. Detection is imperfect, so appeals and records of how work was made start to matter.
uses: If you produce music, audio or video for clients, keep records of your process in case a platform flags it.
Marketing teams using AI music in ads or podcasts: check each platform’s rules before 9 December.
Use AI for drafts and parts, and keep a human-made element, if you publish on platforms with bans.
stories.example: A podcast producer who used an AI tool to sketch a theme tune re-records it with a session musician and keeps the project files in case the track is flagged.
stories.audience: Musicians, labels and distributors, and marketing and content teams that publish audio.
stories.watch: How many tracks are removed after 9 December, false-positive appeals, and whether Spotify or Apple Music move beyond labels.

source.title: TechCrunch: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming, 24 November 2026; Tidal AI Policy
source.quote: at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried

stories.theme: Meta’s Muse agent launches in the UK with British retailers, arrives in Instagram DMs, and shops Walmart’s Black Friday deals in the US
stories.changed: Meta made Muse, its personal AI agent, available to adults in the UK on 24 November 2026 on iOS, Android, muse.ai and WhatsApp. It is free, with paid plans for more use. It launches with UK partners including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Ocado Retail, Trainline, Sainsbury’s, ASOS, easyJet and Jet2. Meta says each Muse runs on its own virtual computer in the cloud, asks before important actions such as sending an email or making a purchase, cannot see passwords or card details, and pays through Onelink by Stripe or Shop Pay. The same day Meta began rolling out Muse inside Instagram DMs in the US, Canada, Mexico, Japan and Singapore, TechCrunch reports, and Walmart said US shoppers can now find and buy its Black Friday deals through Muse. Walmart says Muse gets no access to a customer’s shopping history, and shoppers can set spending limits and require approval before purchases.
stories.matters: Agents that buy things are moving from demos to big retailers, just in time for holiday shopping. Retailers are choosing sides: Walmart opens its store to agents while Amazon has moved to block outside ones.
stories.imply: Expect customers to arrive through agents rather than your website. For shoppers, spending limits and approval steps are the settings that matter.
uses: Retailers: check how your site works when an agent, not a person, searches and fills the basket.
If you try Muse for shopping, set a spending limit and keep approval on for every purchase.
Customer service teams: prepare for refunds and complaints about orders an agent placed.
stories.example: A UK shopper asks Muse to rebook a Trainline journey and reorder a usual Ocado shop, approving each step on the phone before anything is paid.
stories.audience: Retail and e-commerce teams, customer service leads, and consumers in the UK and US trying shopping agents.
stories.watch: Black Friday results from agent shopping, whether more retailers open to agents, and how Amazon responds.

source.title: Meta: Introducing Muse in the UK: A Personal AI Agent You Control, 24 November 2026; TechCrunch on Instagram DMs and Walmart
source.quote: Muse asks for your go-ahead before important actions, like sending an email or making a purchase.

signals.raw: Google Workspace Updates, 24 Nov: Workspace MCP servers (Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, Tasks; Keep soon) and Workspace CLI GA; Admin console Security > API Controls: agent access, HITL confirmation rules, audit logs; DLP applies; AI Tools Addendum (no long-term storage of certain data, no scraping); agents must use MCP not REST from 1 Feb 2027; Standard (free) and Scaled tiers, Scaled billing from 1 Apr 2027; >99% of active developers within Standard; rollout over 2 weeks. Chandu Thota on X: alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway.

OpenClaw blog, 24 Nov (TechCrunch same day): ShellBench, 100 tasks from >10M anonymised agent interactions, 12 models x 5 harnesses, 53,100 graded runs; GPT-6 Astra 62.5% ($1.10/run), Claude Fable 5.2 61.9% ($0.83), GPT-6.1 Sol 61.4% ($0.19), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 39.7% (~5 cents); Astra 75.1% at least once in 3, 48.8% all 3; 15.7% of runs failed a safety check; 9.9% of correct runs failed one; dinner task 522/531 right restaurant, 152 fully passed.

Anthropic, 24 Nov: Install as app (beta) in Claude for Mac and Windows, all plans; own icon/window, Claude + connectors, usage counts to plan; permissions: default (browser-level), app permissions, full computer access; re-asks after every update; full access only for own or same-org apps; no Anthropic review; Team on by default (full access off), Enterprise off until owner enables; not for HIPAA-ready or hybrid deployments. Felix Rieseberg on X.

NCSC blog, 24 Nov: marked rise since Sept 2026 in AI-assisted attacks via agentic offensive frameworks (ARTEX, Cairn, PentAGI, RedAmon, Xalgorix, Darkmoon) with cheap open models or illegal API resellers; exploit old weaknesses (committed credentials, IaC misconfig, default creds, API flaws); discovery to exploitation in minutes; noisy; eight defensive questions incl. exposure inventory, auth proxies, account-level rate limits, secret scanning, honeytokens.

CNBC, 24 Nov: ANT closed down 6.5%, below $83 IPO price; opened $111.50 Thursday; raised $81.3B, largest offering ever. Axios: closed at $81.91, third straight down session. TechCrunch: as low as $76 midday. Canaccord buy $135; Wedbush outperform $120; Oppenheimer outperform $150. Nvidia and chip stocks fell Tuesday after Monday's rally.

Tidal, 24 Nov (TechCrunch, Guardian; Tidal AI Policy updated 24 Nov): from 9 Dec, wholly AI-generated tracks rejected and removed; distributors barred from delivering them; AI-assisted allowed; Robert Anderson on X: 43% of deliveries in last 90 days detected as AI; 27M tracks (6.3%) fully AI, 96% with no streams; demonetised since June; appeals available.
